summary: A republication of RFC 1944 that corrects the IP addresses assigned as defaults for network test equipment. It describes methods for benchmarking network interconnect devices such as routers. It obsoletes RFC 1944 and was updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2544 gives everyone the same rulebook for testing how fast network boxes work, so different vendors' numbers can actually be compared. It fixes the test addresses from the earlier version.

questions: what is a device under test
subtitle: A fixed recipe for testing routers and bridges so vendors' speed claims can be compared fairly.

tldr.problem: Vendors of network devices often make performance claims that can't be compared because they use different testing methods.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common test setup, six standard tests, and how to report results so comparisons are fair and repeatable.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo (not a standard) that obsoletes RFC 1944 and has been updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004.

today: RFC 2544 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1944, and it has been updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004.

sections.title: Why a Standard Benchmark Suite
sections.content:
RFC 2544 opens by naming the problem: vendors often engage in specsmanship to give their products a better position in the marketplace. It defines one set of tests that everyone can run and report, so users get comparable data from different vendors.

The terms come from RFC 1242, which readers should consult first. The RFC says there is no off-the-shelf equipment to run all tests, but such equipment can be built. Not every test applies to every device, and results require judgment about repeatability, variance and statistical significance.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies measure their gear differently to make it look good. This RFC says everyone should run the same tests, so the numbers can be fairly compared.

sections.title: Test Setup, Frames and Device Configuration
sections.content:
The ideal setup is a tester with sending and receiving ports. It sends traffic into the device under test (DUT) and receives it back, so it can verify every frame arrived correctly. Separate sender and receiver machines can work, but may be impractical for some tests.

The DUT MUST be configured as the vendor instructs with all supported protocols enabled, and the configuration MUST NOT be tuned between tests. The software version and exact configuration MUST be reported. Tests SHOULD be run at several frame sizes. For Ethernet the recommended sizes are 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518.

The tester SHOULD discard non-test frames and ideally put sequence numbers in test frames so it can report frames dropped, out of order, duplicated and gaps.
sections.plainLanguage: You put the device in the middle and test it from both sides with known traffic. You can't change the device's settings between tests, and you must record what settings you used.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Trial
sections.content:
Each test consists of trials producing one measurement. A trial follows a fixed sequence: if the DUT is a router, send routing updates and pause two seconds; send learning frames to the output port and wait two seconds; run the test portion; wait two seconds for residual frames; then wait at least five seconds for the DUT to restabilize.

The test portion SHOULD last at least 60 seconds to measure continuous performance. Binary searches may use shorter trials, but final results SHOULD come from full-length trials. Before each trial, a routing update MUST be sent with all network addresses the trial needs, all resolving to the same next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Every test run follows the same steps: get things ready, run for at least 60 seconds, wait for stragglers, and let the device settle. That keeps results consistent.

sections.title: The Six Benchmark Tests
sections.content:
The RFC defines six tests (Section 26). Throughput: the fastest rate at which the received frame count equals the sent frame count (no frame loss). Latency: at throughput rate, send a stream of at least 120 seconds with a tagged frame inserted after 60 seconds; measure time from send to receive and repeat at least 20 times.

Frame loss rate: percentage lost at each input rate, starting at 100% and stepping down by 10% until two successive trials have zero loss. Back-to-back frames: longest burst forwarded with no loss (at least 2-second trials, repeated at least 50 times).

System recovery: overload at 110% of throughput (or media max) for at least 60 seconds, drop to 50%, and measure when last loss occurs. Reset: send at throughput rate, cause a reset, and measure time to resume forwarding (power interruption test lasts 10 seconds).
sections.plainLanguage: There are six checks: how fast with no drops, how long a frame takes to cross, how many drop when pushed, how big a rush it can handle, how fast it recovers from overload, and how fast it comes back after a reset.

sections.title: Reference Data and Test Frames
sections.content:
Appendices give reference values. For example, for 64-byte Ethernet frames the maximum rate is 14880 frames per second; for 1518-byte frames it is 812 frames per second. The test frame is a UDP Echo Request to avoid session setup issues with some routers.

Input ports use Class C networks from 198.18.1.0 to 198.18.64.0 and output ports use 198.19.1.0 to 198.19.64.0, with the router at node 1. These test addresses were corrected from RFC 1944. The RFC does not address security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the rulebook gives reference speeds, a sample test packet, and special addresses to use only for testing. These test addresses are different from the ones in the earlier RFC.
